newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries falter at pricey levels.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries falter at pricey levels.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries drifted lower in a quiet summery session that highlighted the absence of retail interest and Wall Street's caution at pricey levels.

Traders and analysts said the market has already priced in all the good news about the U.S. economy and needed fresh trading incentives to take out some key technical levels, such as the 6.50-percent yield on the 30-year Treasury bond yield.
"A lot of players were out. There just was no buying interest today," said Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler.

"It was very much a day for professionals. Traders were lightening up positions more than anything," Resler said. "There were no incentives to buy, especially with the new supply coming in soon and the fact all the good news has been priced in."
Resler pointed out the main economic reports due out this week -- the June retail sales, Consumer Price Index and industrial production -- were not expected to provide an excuse to rally on.
"The market would almost have to price in an easing of monetary policy to do better," Resler added.
In a Reuters survey, analysts forecast that June retail sales, set for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Tuesday, would be reported up 0.2 percent after a 0.1-percent drop in May.
On Wednesday, the June CPI and its core measure are both expected up 0.2 percent. Industrial production is seen rising 0.2 percent and capacity utilization little changed.

"The market is giving out signs of fatigue ahead of the important retail sales report. There is a special degree of nervousness about the most volatile of economic news," said Resler who pointed out the market's focus is on the demand side -- seen as a key factor in Federal Reserve policy.

Resler said traders were concerned about a possibly large upward revision of the May retail sales data that would underscore the cheerful mood of the American consumer and revive fears of stronger growth and higher interest rates.
Senior economist Astrid Adolfson at MCM MoneyWatch agreed "a few jitters about retail sales took the market lower" late in the session.

"That is what caused a few people to sell. There also was heavy selling in the euros late in the day and some STRIPS selling in the twos," Adolfson remarked. "Otherwise, it was so boring, you could watch the paint dry."
Adolfson said market players were aware Treasuries were expensive at their current levels and that fresh buying warranted caution.
"The 6.50 percent (30-year bond yield) is a tough level," added Adolfson who doubted this big psychological resistance would fall this week, mainly without new cash.
"Investor surveys show people have used a lot of money already," the MCM senior economist pointed out.
"And then, there is supply, with the two- and five-year note auctions next week and the refunding announcement on July 30th. We just go from one thing to another," she added.
In late trading, the 30-year bond was down 10/32 at 100-30/32 to yield 6.55 percent.
The two-year note was down 3/32 at 100-4/32 to yield 5.93 percent, the five-year note down 5/32 at 100-12/32 and 6.16 percent. The 10-year note closed down 7/32 at 102-22/32 and 6.25 percent.
Also, the three-month bill was up two basis points to a rate of 5.01 percent. The six-month bill was up one at 5.11 percent and the year-bill up two at 5.24 percent.
